title: What is man (Psalm 8)
hookLine: the stars, and yet God is mindful of us

cards: A farm road at night, far from any town. The car door shuts, the headlights go off, and someone looks up. There are far too many stars.
The Milky Way is a smear of light across the whole sky. All of that, and one person on a patch of gravel with cold hands.
Someone once stood under that same sky, without telescopes, without knowing how far away any of it was, and asked the question out loud.

teach.b: Psalm 8 opens and closes with nearly the same line, like two hands cupped around it: "O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth!" In between, the question.
"For I will behold thy heavens, the works of thy fingers: the moon and the stars which thou hast founded." Fingers. Not arms, not great labor: the whole night sky as fingerwork, like embroidery.
Then: "What is man that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man that thou visitest him?" The Hebrew word for man here, enosh, has the sense of a frail human, someone mortal and breakable.
The question isn't philosophical. It's astonished. Why would the one who made all that bother to remember this?

teach.h: A LITTLE LESS THAN THE ANGELS.
teach.b: Then the psalm turns the smallness inside out: "Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, thou hast crowned him with glory and honour."
One detail: the Hebrew says a little less than elohim, a word that can mean God, or gods, or heavenly beings.
The old Greek translators chose angels, the Latin and the Douay followed, and the Letter to the Hebrews quotes it that way about Jesus. The Church reads both: every human being small, and crowned.

teach.h: THE PSALM WENT TO THE MOON.
teach.b: In 1969 the Apollo 11 astronauts left a small disc on the moon with messages from world leaders, and Pope Paul VI's words on it quoted this psalm. The words went all the way up to the thing the psalm was looking at.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 8 in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, including on the feast of the Holy Trinity in some years; the Letter to the Hebrews applies its words to Jesus.

s: Psalm 8 begins and ends with nearly the same line
O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name: it opens the psalm, and almost word for word, it closes it.
the Hebrew clearly says a little less than the angels
it says elohim, which can mean God, gods or heavenly beings. the Greek chose angels.
the psalm calls the stars the work of God's arms
the work of thy fingers, like fine handwork.

games.q: you're standing under a sky full of stars and you feel tiny. where does Psalm 8 take that feeling?
o: it asks why God remembers us, then says we're crowned with glory.
it says the stars are gods.
games.why: what is man that thou art mindful of him? then: thou hast crowned him with glory and honour. small, and remembered.

practice: If it's night, step outside or go to a window; if it's daytime, close your eyes and remember the darkest, starriest sky you've ever seen.
Notice how big it is and how small one person is beside it, without hurrying past, then hold the psalm's other half alongside: small, and still remembered.
If you pray, say its first line, O Lord our Lord; if you don't, just stay with the size of things.

wordCard.voice: Enosh. Hebrew for a frail, mortal human, the psalm's word for the question under the stars: why would God remember someone so small? Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: what is man. enosh has the sense of a frail, mortal human.

carryVoice: Your line: small, and remembered. Both at once, under the same sky. That's day one hundred sixty.
